To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) PMC and economic growth rates are ambiguously correlated if the returns to specialization are declining, whereas they are positively correlated when returns to specializations are increasing; (ii) population and economic growth are positively correlated if returns to specialization are rising, whereas they are negatively correlated if the returns are decreasing; and (iii) the returns to specialization can be decreasing or increasing depending on whether the production complexity is increasing or decreasing.
the effects of PMC and population on economic growth depend on whether returns to specialization are positive or negative.
(i) the effect of competition on growth depends on whether returns to specialization are positive or negative; and (ii) the effect of population on growth depends on returns to specialization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of returns to specialization in explaining the relationship between PMC, population, and economic growth.
the effects of specialization and competition on the rate of technological progress.
the effects that the use of more varieties of intermediate goods has on the growth rate of the economy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PMC, population and economic growth are positively and ambiguously correlated.

, in our model, the correlation between economic growth rates and population growth rates is ambiguous, while the correlation between economic-growth and PMC is ambiguous only if returns to specialization are not decreasing.

the relationship between economic growth and PMC (and between economic growth and population) depends on returns to specialization, and that these returns are increasing when the number of varieties used in the production process is larger.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, under the assumptions of the model, the effects of PMC on growth, and of population on growth, may be either positive, negative, or zero, depending on the nature of the returns-to-specialization function.
, in a world of increasing returns to specialization, population growth and PMC are positively correlated with economic growth.

the correlation between PMC and growth, or between population and growth, is positive if the production-complexity effect is positive, but negative if the production-complementarity effect is positive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in a world where the number of intermediate-input goods is not fixed, the relationship between economic growth rates and PMC or population growth rates is not necessarily positive or negative.
the correlation between PMC and economic growth, on the one hand, and population and economic growth, is ambiguous and depends on the returns to specialization.
the correlation between PMC, economic growth and population growth is not a robust prediction of the model.
